And so over time, citizens become much tougher and more unified. In contrast, the Carthaginians grow corrupt and decadent. Because Romans are deeply invested in the war, they fight until the end. Conversely, Carthaginians are primarily traders known for their business acumen. They conduct cost-benefit analyses, concluding that continuing the war would be costlier than surrendering. Thus, the Carthaginians surrendered after the First Punic War and later in the Second and Third Punic Wars.

Guess what happens? The Romans will enslave them. This reflects Roman brutality—they fight to the death and if they win, all of you will die. That’s their mentality. Eventually, Rome conquers Carthage despite initial uncertainty about its history. A key moment is when Hannibal Barca crosses the Alps with his army and elephants into Italy to attack Rome directly.

In three crucial battles, Hannibal decisively defeats Roman forces. He sends an envoy to the Senate offering peace terms after destroying every Roman soldier, but they refuse. This marks a pivotal point in Roman history. Key events include Hannibal's crossing of the Alps, one of the most famous military feats; the Battle of Trivia where he ambushed Romans using cavalry; and the Battle of Lake Trebia where his strategy again outmaneuvered the Romans.

The battles at Lake Trasimene and Cannae are infamous. At Cannae, Hannibal uses a double-envelopment tactic: sending cavalry on both wings to encircle the Roman army, then trapping them from behind. This results in massive Roman casualties—between 50,000 to 100,000 soldiers lost, wiping out their entire army.

Theoretically, Romans should have been motivated by the danger of drowning but instead were overwhelmed and defeated by Hannibal's superior tactics.
